extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in U.S. civil liberties and ACLU history
extracted.subtask_description: A historical overview of the American Civil Liberties Union highlighting key legal standards, organizational policies, case-selection considerations, and strategic shifts across decades. The page records landmark court tests, ACLU policy statements, and practical examples used to explain the organization's positions and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to guilt by association and judgment by accusation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU 'stand[s] against guilt by association, judgment by accusation, the invasion of privacy of personal opinions and beliefs, and the confusion of dissent with disloyalty'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of organizational principle used to justify defending unpopular or accused individuals/groups; provides normative guidance for case selection and public messaging (example context: response to anti-communist purges in mid-20th century).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brandenburg/imminent-violence test for outlawing speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Only speech which advocated imminent violence could be outlawed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal standard articulated in Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) and referenced as a limiting principle on criminalizing speech; used to evaluate whether advocacy crosses constitutionally-prohibited incitement (example: protection even of KKK member's advocacy unless it advocated imminent violence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-prong obscenity test (obscenity standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Child pornography (and obscenity) should be evaluated under the 'three prong obscenity test' to determine whether it is outlawed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced in New York v. Ferber context: ACLU argued that material violating the three-prong test could be banned, but cautioned that overly broad laws risked banning artistic/non-obscene material. Historical example shows tension between protecting children and avoiding overbroad censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior restraint prohibition on pre-publication censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may not preemptively prohibit publication; it must wait until after publication to take action (no prior restraint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes the principle from New York Times Co. v. United States (Pentagon Papers): used to evaluate government attempts to block publication of classified information; supports ACLU litigation against prior restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to privacy as judicially recognized standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to privacy, though not explicit in the Constitution, has been established by the Court (e.g., Griswold v. Connecticut) and underpins reproductive rights (e.g., Roe v. Wade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames ACLU advocacy on contraception, abortion, and medical decision-making; used as a substantive constitutional criterion when challenging statutes restricting intimate decisions or governmental access to personal records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of rights within 'enclaves' (schools, prisons, mental hospitals, military)
rubrics_metrics.description: People in government-run 'enclaves' (schools, prisons, military facilities, mental hospitals) nonetheless retain constitutional protections; schools may not be 'enclaves' where all rights are forfeited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originates from Tinker v. Des Moines and related doctrine (Abe Fortas phrase). Guides litigation strategy for students, prisoners, mental health patients, and military members—used to decide when to bring cases asserting retained rights in controlled institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warrant requirement for searches of homes (exclusionary protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: States must obtain a warrant before searching a person's home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Mapp v. Ohio (1961) — a clear procedural constitutional requirement limiting police powers and guiding ACLU challenges to unlawful searches and evidence admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to appointed counsel for indigent defendants
rubrics_metrics.description: Indigent criminal defendants have a right to legal representation (right to counsel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes Gideon v. Wainwright (1963); used to evaluate adequacy of criminal representation and to bring suits when states fail to provide counsel to those who cannot afford it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to counsel during interrogation (Escobedo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspects have a right to have an attorney present during questioning in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Escobedo v. Illinois (1964); used as a criterion to challenge custodial interrogations and coerced statements. Forms part of broader protections against police overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miranda warnings and extension to juveniles
rubrics_metrics.description: Police must notify suspects of their constitutional rights (Miranda), and those protections were later extended to juveniles (In re Gault).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miranda v. Arizona (1966) requires advising of rights to silence and counsel; In re Gault (1967) extended certain procedural protections to juveniles — used when assessing validity of custodial confessions and juvenile adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard limiting involuntary psychiatric confinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Involuntary commitments are unlawful unless it can be demonstrated that the person is a danger to himself or the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounded in ACLU litigation and O'Connor v. Donaldson (1975) — used to challenge long-term non-consensual confinement of non-dangerous mentally ill individuals and to craft statutes respecting due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-selection consideration: extent to which defending a case may assist extremists/opponents of ACLU values
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding whether to take a case affiliates should consider 'the extent to which the speech may assist in advancing the goals of white supremacists or others whose views are contrary to our values.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extracted from an internal (June 2018) ACLU memo presented as a guideline to affiliates — not a change in official policy per the memo's authors. Used as a practical factor in evaluating whether to provide representation or support, with examples referenced (cases defending hateful or antisemitic protesters).

rubrics_metrics.name: National security policy standard: consistency with Constitution, rule of law, and human rights
rubrics_metrics.description: National security policies must be consistent with the Constitution, the rule of law, and fundamental human rights; 'Liberty and security do not compete in a zero-sum game.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement from the ACLU's National Security Project guiding challenges to counterterrorism measures (e.g., Patriot Act litigation). Used to assess whether security measures violate due process, privacy, illegal search protections, or constitute cruel and unusual punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness/uncertainty doctrine against undefined statutory terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of undefined terms like 'indecent' and 'patently offensive' in statutes provokes uncertainty among speakers and can render laws constitutionally problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes Court reasoning in Reno v. ACLU (1997) invalidating certain CDA provisions; used to evaluate and litigate against statutes that are vague or overbroad in regulating speech online or in media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to defend unpopular or repugnant speech as First Amendment principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU has historically defended speech it finds repugnant (e.g., KKK, Nazis, Westboro) to uphold First Amendment protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Skokie, Westboro picketing cases) illustrate the organizational commitment and the political/financial consequences (membership losses, fundraising) of defending offensive speech; this functions as an institutional criterion for when to litigate despite anticipated backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical/organizational criteria: shift from amicus briefs to direct representation and creation of project-focused litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 1960s–1970s the ACLU shifted emphasis from Supreme Court amicus briefs to direct representation of defendants at arrest and created focused projects (e.g., Women's Rights Project, Reproductive Freedom Project) to advance specific categories of rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes strategic criteria for maximizing impact: choosing direct representation for frontline cases; forming specialized projects to concentrate expertise and resources (examples: Women's Rights Project, Reproductive Freedom Project).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to laws or policies that interfere with access to information or communication (e.g., internet filtering, bans)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACLU challenges government or institutional actions that block access to information or censor speech (examples: lawsuits against library internet filtering policies; opposition to banning social media platforms on First Amendment grounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited examples include suits against library filtering (blocking pro-gun sites/Google Images) and public opposition to platform bans (TikTok); used as an evaluative principle when determining whether policies unlawfully restrict access to protected speech or information.
